questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is deciding which injections she may give in the pharmacy under the Department's current administration guidance. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A long-acting injectable antipsychotic such as paliperidone palmitate is eligible.
Testosterone for gender-affirming care is eligible, in any of its salts.
Cabotegravir for prevention of HIV is eligible for administration.
Any long-acting injectable is eligible, since the list gives examples of the class.
The pharmacist is not obliged to administer an eligible medication on request.

questions.stem: A patient asks a Massachusetts community pharmacist to administer methadone for addiction treatment. The patient presents a valid prescription from a practitioner, and the pharmacist has completed injection training and holds current CPR certification. May the pharmacist administer it there?

choices.text: Yes, because the pharmacist holds a valid prescription for the patient.
Yes, because the pharmacist has completed the required training and certification.
No, because that administration may occur only in a registered opioid treatment program.
No, because a pharmacist may never administer any medication for addiction treatment.
No, unless the prescriber attends the pharmacy at the time of administration.

questions.stem: A prescription for an eligible long-acting injectable arrives at a Massachusetts pharmacy without the administration notation the Department's guidance asks prescribers to include. In the pharmacist's judgment the product is plainly intended to be given in the pharmacy rather than handed to the patient. What does the guidance call for?

choices.text: The pharmacist is encouraged to contact the prescriber, and administration stays open.
The pharmacist must refuse to administer until a corrected prescription arrives.
The pharmacist must dispense the product to the patient rather than administer it.
The pharmacist must obtain the prescriber's written confirmation before proceeding.
The pharmacist must record the omission and report it to the Board within 24 hours.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is asked to give an eligible medication in the pharmacy. Which statements about the permitted route are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: An intravenous infusion is permitted where the pharmacist is trained to place a line.
Any parenteral route is permitted so long as the product label allows it.
The route is at the pharmacist's professional discretion for an eligible product.
Administration must accord with manufacturer approved labeling for the product.
Only subcutaneous or intramuscular injection is permitted.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts prescriber writes for an eligible injectable to be administered in the pharmacy, specifying a single dose with three refills. The pharmacy manager says the refills make the prescription unusable for administration because the conditions require single doses. Who is right?

choices.text: The manager, because refills convert it into a course of therapy.
The manager, because each administration needs its own prescription.
The manager, unless the prescriber confirms the intent in writing.
The pharmacist, because single-dose prescribing may carry refills.
The pharmacist, because the single-dose condition governs packaging only.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist rounding in a licensed long-term care facility decides to start a controlled substance for a resident. She writes what looks like an ordinary outpatient prescription and leaves it at the nurses' station. What does the regulation require instead?

choices.text: A prescription transmitted to the facility's contracted dispensing pharmacy.
A written medication order entered on the facility's own medical record for the resident.
A countersignature from the supervising physician on the prescription she wrote.
An oral order to the nurse on duty, confirmed in writing within 24 hours.
A referral back to the supervising physician, who must issue the order himself.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist provides services on site at an assisted living residence that holds no health facility licence. She proposes to use a written medication order entered on the residence's own care record, as she does when working in a licensed hospice. What is the position?

choices.text: Permitted, because a written order is more rigorous than a prescription.
Permitted, because the residence maintains a care record for each resident.
Permitted, provided the supervising physician approves the residence in the agreement.
Not permitted, because the medication order route is unavailable outside a facility.
Not permitted, because a pharmacist may not provide services at a residence at all.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist plans to hold stock for dispensing for immediate treatment under her agreement. Which statements about how she may obtain it are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Any product she may prescribe may be bought from her usual wholesaler.
A Schedule IV product may be bought from a wholesaler for this purpose.
Schedule VI products she is authorised to prescribe may be ordered from a wholesaler.
Schedule II to V products may be bought from a distributor if properly recorded.
Schedule II to V products may come from the supervising physician or a patient's order.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist holds a Department registration for the purpose of prescribing and a valid agreement. She wishes to dispense a Schedule VI product for immediate treatment. That particular product is not among those her agreement authorises her to prescribe. May she do so?

choices.text: Yes, because immediate treatment is a separate power from prescribing.
Yes, because the product sits in Schedule VI, the least restricted schedule.
Yes, provided she notifies the supervising physician within 24 hours.
No, because the power runs only to substances she is authorised to prescribe.
No, because dispensing for immediate treatment requires a patient-specific order.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborative practice agreement authorises the pharmacist to modify the dosage of a named medication for a referred patient. Reviewing the patient, the pharmacist judges the medication should be stopped altogether. The agreement says nothing about stopping therapy. What may she do?

choices.text: She may not discontinue it, because that act must itself be authorised.
She may discontinue it, because stopping is a lesser step than modifying.
She may discontinue it, because it is a clinical rather than a prescribing act.
She may discontinue it once she notes the reason in the patient's record.
She may discontinue it only where the medication is in Schedule VI.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist holds a current Department controlled substance registration that she obtained so that her pharmacy could dispense. She now has a valid collaborative practice agreement that includes prescriptive practices, and proposes to issue her first prescription. What does she still need?

choices.text: Nothing further; her current registration covers controlled substance activity.
A separate Board of Registration in Pharmacy licence category for prescribers.
The supervising physician's registration number recorded in the agreement.
A DEA registration, which is required for every collaborating pharmacist.
Department registration for the purpose of prescribing under 105 CMR 700.000.

questions.stem: Two Massachusetts collaborating pharmacists each hold Department registration for the purpose of prescribing. One will prescribe only Schedule VI products under her agreement. The other will prescribe products in federally controlled schedules. Neither holds a DEA registration. What follows?

choices.text: Both are barred, because the regulation requires DEA registration of prescribers.
Neither is barred, because Department registration is the operative requirement.
The first may prescribe; the second needs DEA registration because it applies.
The second may prescribe; the first needs DEA registration for Schedule VI.
Both may prescribe, provided each notifies the DEA of the agreement's terms.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist practising collaboratively in a retail drug business is reviewing what the statute permits her to do there. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Patients must be 18 years of age or older in that setting.
She may initiate new therapy for a referred patient's primary diagnosis.
She may extend current therapy prescribed by the supervising physician by 30 days.
She may modify dosages of any medication the patient is currently taking.
She may administer vaccines under the terms of her agreement.

questions.stem: A referred patient at a Massachusetts retail pharmacy has run out of a medication her supervising physician prescribed, and the physician is unreachable. The collaborating pharmacist has never dispensed this patient a different medication for the same condition. What may the pharmacist do under the retail collaborative power?

choices.text: Initiate an equivalent medication for the same condition for up to 30 days.
Extend the current therapy the supervising physician prescribed by 30 days.
Extend the current therapy indefinitely until the physician can be reached.
Substitute a therapeutically similar agent and notify the physician afterwards.
Nothing, because the retail setting confers no continuation power at all.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts health system is setting up collaborative drug therapy management across several of its sites. Which statements about who must approve it are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: In a licensed hospital, the Department of Public Health approves the arrangement.
A single system-wide approval suffices for every one of the listed settings.
In a long-term care facility, the facility's medical director or designee approves.
In a hospice setting, the hospice's medical director or designee approves.
An ambulatory care clinic additionally requires on-site physician supervision.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts ambulatory care clinic has obtained approval from its medical staff executive committee for collaborative drug therapy management. The collaborating pharmacist works remotely from another site, reviewing records and speaking to patients by telephone. No physician is present with her. Is the arrangement compliant?

choices.text: Yes, because the correct approving body has approved the arrangement.
Yes, because the statute does not regulate where the pharmacist works.
Yes, provided the attending physician is reachable during clinic hours.
No, because the clinic setting requires on-site supervision by the attending physician.
No, because collaborative practice may not be conducted in an ambulatory care clinic.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist holds a current collaborative practice agreement that authorises her to administer vaccines. There is no Commissioner order in force for any designated vaccine, and the vaccine she is asked to give is not on the Department's eligible-medication administration list. May she give it?

choices.text: Yes, because the collaborative practice agreement authorises vaccine administration.
Yes, because vaccines fall outside the controlled substance framework entirely.
No, because a Commissioner order is needed before any vaccine may be given.
No, because the vaccine is absent from the eligible-medication list.
No, because a pharmacist may administer vaccines only in a hospital setting.

questions.stem: A busy Massachusetts pharmacy decides that patients wanting the pharmacist to prescribe a hormonal contraceptive must book a slot in advance so the pharmacist can plan her day. Walk-ins are told to come back at a booked time. Is that policy permissible?

choices.text: Yes, because appointment scheduling is ordinary workflow management.
Yes, provided the earliest available slot is within seven days.
Yes, provided the pharmacy also offers a walk-in service one day a week.
No, because the patient must instead be referred to a prescriber.
No, because requiring an appointment for this service is prohibited.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist has just prescribed and dispensed a self-administered oral hormonal contraceptive after completing the required screening. Which duties attach at that point? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Refer the patient to her primary care or reproductive health care practitioner, if applicable.
Alternatively advise the patient to consult with such a practitioner.
Provide the patient with a written record of what was prescribed and dispensed.
Obtain the practitioner's agreement before the supply may be handed over.
Dispense as soon as practicable after issuing the prescription.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist completes the screening and issues a prescription for a hormonal contraceptive patch on a Friday afternoon. She tells the patient the pharmacy will order the product and asks her to return the following week to collect it, although an equivalent product is in stock. Is that consistent with the statute?

choices.text: Yes, because the prescribing duty and the dispensing decision are separate.
Yes, because the patient suffers no clinical detriment from a short wait.
Yes, provided the pharmacist gives the patient the written record on the Friday.
No, because the statute requires dispensing as soon as practicable after issuing.
No, because a pharmacist may not issue a prescription she cannot fill that day.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy proposes to run a walk-in clinic for a newly designated vaccine during a public health event. Which statements about what must be in place are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A practitioner standing prescription alone opens this pathway.
The Commissioner must determine that health care professionals will be insufficient.
A Commissioner order authorizing the administration removes any need for a prescription.
Administration must accord with the Commissioner's order as well as a practitioner instrument.
A designation of the vaccine by the Commissioner is required.

questions.stem: A Commissioner order authorising administration of a designated vaccine is in force in Massachusetts. A pharmacy wishes to use a student enrolled in an approved programme for licensure as a health care professional to help administer doses. What does the regulation require for the student?

choices.text: The student may act on the same footing as a licensed professional.
The student must be authorised and supervised by a licensed qualified professional.
The student may not administer vaccine under this pathway in any circumstances.
The student must hold a separate Department certification before assisting.
The student may act only where the pharmacy notifies the Commissioner first.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy operating under a Commissioner order holds training records and a written plan for responding to adverse events. Which further protocol subjects does the regulation require it to cover? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Proper storage of vaccine.
Marketing of the vaccination service to patients.
Return of unused vaccine.
Reimbursement arrangements for administered doses.
Recordkeeping regarding administration.

questions.stem: An electronically transmitted oxycodone prescription reaches a Massachusetts outpatient pharmacy for a patient whose voluntary non-opiate directive is recorded in the system. The pharmacist on duty never opens the record, does not know of the directive, and dispenses. What is her position under the statute?

choices.text: In violation, because the directive was recorded and available to her.
In violation, because failing to check the record is at least negligent.
In violation, because the prescription contradicted a filed directive.
Not in violation only if the pharmacy has no system for surfacing directives.
Not in violation, because she is protected unless she acted knowingly against it.

questions.stem: In the same Massachusetts health system, an outpatient pharmacist carelessly dispenses an opiate contrary to a filed non-opiate directive without knowing of it, and a nurse practitioner carelessly administers one to the same patient without checking. Neither acted knowingly. How do their positions compare under the section?

choices.text: Both are protected, because neither of them acted knowingly against the directive.
Both are exposed, because carelessness is enough for a licensing board to act.
The pharmacist is exposed and the practitioner is protected on these facts.
Both turn on whether the patient suffered harm from the opiate administered.
The pharmacist is protected and the practitioner is exposed to board action.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist is issuing a prescription that another pharmacy will fill. Which particulars must she supply to the dispensing pharmacist? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Her home address, so that she can be reached outside working hours.
Her date of initial licensure in the Commonwealth.
Her registration number.
The name of her supervising physician.
Confirmation that the patient has consented to collaborative management.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist takes a telephoned prescription from a collaborating pharmacist who gives her name, professional designation, registration number, work address and a callback number, but does not name the supervising physician. What should the receiving pharmacist do?

choices.text: Fill it, because the caller supplied the identifying particulars that matter.
Fill it, and record that the supervising physician was not identified.
Decline to fill it as transmitted until the supervising physician is named.
Decline to fill it, because a pharmacist may not telephone a prescription at all.
Fill it, provided she verifies the caller's registration number independently.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist and a physician working in the same clinic each point to M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9 as their authority to hold and give a controlled substance. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The section authorises possession of what is reasonably required for patient treatment.
It authorises administration, or causing administration under direction by a nurse.
The pharmacist appears in the section on the same footing as the physician.
The pharmacist appears only as limited by other named provisions.
Registration under section 7 is unnecessary where the practitioner acts in good faith.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist with no collaborative practice agreement, registered under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7, wishes to keep a stock of a controlled substance for patient treatment and to administer it, relying on s. 9 alone. A physician in the same clinic, registered on the same basis, proposes to do the same. How do their positions differ?

choices.text: They do not differ; both are authorised by the same sentence of section 9.
They do not differ; both need a collaborative practice agreement to proceed.
The pharmacist may proceed and the physician needs a further instrument.
Neither may proceed, because section 9 confers no possession authority at all.
The physician may proceed; the pharmacist is limited by two further provisions.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy dispenses emergency contraception, opioid antagonists and COVID-19 control measures under the respective standing orders. Which statements about its reporting duties are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A single combined annual return satisfies all three regimes.
Opioid antagonist doses dispensed are reported annually.
COVID-19 control measures are reported to the department upon request.
Emergency contraception is reported only when the department opens an inquiry.
Each report must identify the individual patients supplied.

questions.stem: A journalist makes a public records request to a Massachusetts department for the reports a named pharmacy filed about opioid antagonists it dispensed. The pharmacy asks its pharmacist what the statutory position is. What should the pharmacist say?

choices.text: The reports are public records once filed with a state agency.
The reports are public records with patient identifiers redacted.
The reports are available only to the prescriber who issued the standing order.
The reports are confidential and are not public records under the statute.
The reports may be released once the department publishes its annual summary.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is asked in one shift to administer a long-acting injectable antipsychotic, testosterone for gender-affirming care, and an antibiotic for a sexually transmitted infection. Which statements about the statutory basis for each are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: All three rest on the same statutory clause and share the same conditions.
The antipsychotic route requires the direction of a prescribing practitioner.
The antipsychotic route additionally requires departmental regulations.
The testosterone route rests on a prescription for that purpose.
The sexually transmitted infection route rests on a prescription for that purpose.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist learns informally that her supervising physician surrendered his federal controlled substances registration last month. His medical licence is unrestricted and she has received no notice from any board. May she continue co-managing patients this afternoon?

choices.text: No, because the physician is deemed ineligible on that surrender alone.
Yes, because his medical licence remains unrestricted.
Yes, because no board has notified her that anything has changed.
Yes, because only a state registration event affects the collaboration.
Yes, provided she confines herself to non-controlled therapies today.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is reviewing a proposed collaborative practice agreement before signing it. Which features does the statutory definition require for the agreement to be validly constituted? Select all that apply.

choices.text: It must be written and signed by the pharmacist and the supervising physician.
The collaborative practice may extend beyond the supervising physician's own scope.
It is subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis.
It must be filed with the Board before the pharmacist may act under it.
It must include individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist has been on duty for twelve hours when the relief pharmacist calls in sick and three patients are waiting on urgent therapy. Her district manager tells her to stay until the queue clears. Which statements about her continuing are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: She may continue only as an extenuating circumstance in the patient's interest.
The time she works beyond twelve hours must be minimized.
She must document the extenuating circumstance that justified continuing.
The manager's instruction is itself sufficient authority for her to continue.
The twelve hour ceiling binds pharmacists but not certified pharmacy technicians.
